clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of acute kidney injury in multiple myeloma, from precipitation of monoclonal free light chains in the tubules
It presents as acute or subacute kidney injury, often precipitated by dehydration, hypercalcaemia, infection or nephrotoxins
The urine dipstick is typically negative for protein because it detects albumin, not the light chains
Serum free light chain assay and serum/urine electrophoresis are key to diagnosis
Precipitating factors such as hypercalcaemia and nephrotoxic drugs should be corrected urgently
Rapid reduction of the offending light chains with anti-myeloma therapy offers the best chance of renal recovery
reference.pathophysiology: In cast nephropathy, an excess of monoclonal free light chains produced by a plasma cell neoplasm is filtered and reaches the distal tubule, where they bind Tamm-Horsfall protein and precipitate to form obstructing tubular casts. The casts cause intratubular obstruction and a local inflammatory and toxic injury to tubular cells. Volume depletion, hypercalcaemia, loop diuretics and nephrotoxins promote cast formation, so these factors both precipitate and worsen the injury. Reducing the circulating light chain burden is central to reversing it.
additionalDifferentials: Other myeloma-related renal disease (light chain deposition disease, AL amyloidosis)
Contrast or drug-induced acute kidney injury
Acute tubular necrosis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Serum free light chain assay and serum/urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation
Renal function, calcium and urinalysis (often dipstick-negative for protein)
Full blood count and bone marrow assessment for myeloma
Identification and correction of precipitating factors
redFlags: Severe or dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury
Very high free light chain levels
reference.prognosis: Renal recovery is possible if light chains are reduced rapidly and precipitants corrected early, but delayed treatment or prolonged injury can lead to dialysis dependence.
pitfalls: Being falsely reassured by a negative urine dipstick for protein
Failing to check free light chains in unexplained acute kidney injury in older patients
Not correcting hypercalcaemia and volume depletion urgently
Continuing nephrotoxins that promote cast formation
management: Rapid reduction of the circulating monoclonal free light chains with bortezomib-based anti-myeloma chemotherapy
Aggressive intravenous rehydration to reverse volume depletion and reduce intratubular cast formation
Correction of hypercalcaemia and withdrawal of nephrotoxins and loop diuretics
Renal replacement therapy for established severe acute kidney injury, with consideration of high cut-off haemodialysis to remove light chains
Monitoring of the serum free light chain response and renal function to gauge recovery
Avoidance of further precipitants including iodinated contrast and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
